name: Freya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a flow-wrapper on the packing line at Haldane Biscuits. That's the machine that wraps each stack of biscuits in film and seals the ends. I feed the film roll, keep the stacks lined up, and stop the line when the seal goes crooked, which is most mornings. I've been there a year and a half, and I still get flustered when the film snaps and everyone's waiting on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home with you, and how are you fixed for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The smell is the best bit, honestly, warm sugar all day. The worst bit is the bosses changing things. A bigger food group bought Haldane last year, and since then there's a new form for everything. I don't use those AI apps, I don't even like the self-checkout at the supermarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone and let us get on with it. At work everyone would agree with that. I don't post online much, so I'd just say it to Lukas over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm relieved, but the new owners still worry me. AI or no AI, the new owners closed a factory up north and moved the work somewhere cheaper. That could happen to us at the biscuit factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job well, so I'm not on any list. I'd keep the two and a half months we've got saved and not touch it. Maybe I'd start keeping an eye on jobs at the crisp factory across the ring road, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but still with a knot in my stomach about the new owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lukas do, and does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas, my partner, drives a bus for the council, which is steady. His job keeps the rent paid if mine wobbles, but not much more than that. We're not rich, we just don't spend much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work do you talk to about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mainly Bev on the next machine. She's been there twenty years and says owners come and go. She makes me feel better, but then I remember the factory up north.

say: I'd say **leave us alone** and let us get on with it.
I'd mostly just say it to Lukas (my partner) **over dinner**.
think: Privately, **the new owners** worry me more than AI ever did.
They already **closed a factory** up north and moved the work somewhere cheaper.
do: Keep my head down and **do the job well** to stay off any list.
Leave the **savings** of two and a half months untouched.
Watch for openings at **the crisp factory** across the ring road.
feel: Relieved, but with **a knot** about the new owners.
S0.quote: AI or no AI, the new owners closed a factory up north and moved the work somewhere cheaper. That could happen to us at the biscuit factory.
fieldNote: Her worry is **the takeover**, which AI Plateau does nothing to ease.
She avoids technology in daily life, down to **the self-checkout**.
Bev (a twenty-year colleague) is her **main reassurance** at work.

steps.text: Keep running the flow-wrapper without mistakes to stay off any cut list
Leave the joint savings untouched for emergencies
Watch job adverts at the crisp factory across the ring road

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem first, and I'd say it a bit smugly. Then I'd say the robots will come for us after, and someone has to keep an eye on that. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the new owners will use it as an excuse. They'll say AI does the planning now, so they need fewer supervisors, and then the cuts creep down to the line. I'm one of the slowest on the wrapper, so I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get faster on the wrapper, maybe ask Bev to show me her tricks on a quiet shift. We'd stop eating out and cancel the streaming services, to stretch the savings. I'd look at the crisp factory properly, and maybe the meat plant, but I wouldn't jump unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and annoyed that I'd have to think about it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the AI tools, if the factory asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd do it, but I wouldn't be good at it. I can barely work the new tablet on the line, the one where you log stoppages. I'd need someone to sit next to me and be patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways on Friday, then the streaming. Lukas would grumble about the football channel. We'd keep the car because I'm on early shifts and the bus doesn't start in time.

say: I'd say it's **the office's problem** first, a little smugly.
Then I'd say **the robots** will come for us later.
think: Privately, the new owners will use AI **as an excuse** to cut.
I'm one of **the slowest** on the wrapper, so I'd be at risk.
do: Ask Bev to show me **faster tricks** on the wrapper during quiet shifts.
Cancel **takeaways and streaming** to stretch the savings.
Look properly at **other factories** nearby but only move if forced.
feel: **Anxious**, and annoyed I'd have to think about it.
S1.quote: I can barely work the new tablet on the line, the one where you log stoppages. I'd need someone to sit next to me and be patient.
fieldNote: She expects the owners to use **AI as cover** for cuts.
Her resistance is honest: she'd learn **only if made to**.
Spending cuts are already **ranked**, with the car kept for early shifts.

steps.text: Ask Bev to teach her faster film changes on quiet shifts
Cancel Friday takeaways and the streaming services
Compare jobs at the crisp factory and meat plant without applying yet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should slow it down. At work we'd all be saying the same thing, and nobody would know what to do. I'd probably just say it to Lukas and my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished at Haldane by 2031. The ordering and planning go in 2028, and the owners will be even quicker to cut corners. In three years a robot would do what I do on the biscuit line, and it doesn't snap the film every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent, food or the car, straight away. I'd try to get a job somewhere with people in it, maybe a care home kitchen, because that feels further from robots. In the first year I'd probably just hang on at Haldane and hope I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I feel sick thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap of three years before the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have three years of knowing it's coming and not knowing what to do. Some people would use that time well. I'd probably spend it worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Lukas's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buses would be driving themselves by then, wouldn't they? So we'd both be looking for work. I'd ask my mum if we could move back in with her if it came to it.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and someone should slow it down.
I'd mostly say it to **Lukas and my mum**, not online.
think: Privately, I expect to be **finished at Haldane** by 2031.
A robot will wrap biscuits and **never snap the film**.
do: Cut spending to **essentials only**: rent, food and the car.
Look for work with people in it, like **a care home kitchen**.
**Hang on at Haldane** in the first year and hope I'm wrong.
feel: **Frightened**, to the point of feeling sick.
S2.quote: In three years a robot would do what I do on the biscuit line, and it doesn't snap the film every morning.
fieldNote: She sees the three-year gap as **three years of dread**, not a chance.
Both household jobs feel exposed, as Lukas (her partner) **drives a bus**.
Her fallback is **family**: moving back in with her mum.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and the car
Apply for kitchen jobs at local care homes
Stay at Haldane through the first year and watch for cuts
Ask her mum about moving back in if both jobs go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not long, and I'd wonder why nobody's doing anything. At work we'd joke about the robots, but it wouldn't be funny. I'd keep it off the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years sounds like a lot, but robots by 2034 still means I'm out of the wrapper job in my thirties. I'd have time, but I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe get us to four months. I'd ask around about the care home kitchen or a cleaning job at the hospital, places with people. I'd probably wait a year or two before moving, to see if it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Five years is a slower car crash, but still a car crash. I'm not good at learning new stuff, so I'm not sure what I'd use the time for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't like jumping, and I'd want to see the robots actually working first. If I leave Haldane and the new place shuts, I'd feel stupid. Bev says the ones who panic always regret it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something sensible, like paying people while they learn something else. I don't want handouts forever, I just want a bit of time. Both sides would probably argue about it and nothing would happen.

say: I'd say five years **isn't long** and ask why nobody's acting.
At work we'd **joke about the robots**, without it being funny.
think: Privately, robots by **2034** still push me out of the wrapper job in my thirties.
I'm **not good at learning** new things, so the extra time may not help.
do: Save harder to reach **four months** of expenses.
Ask about **care home kitchen** or hospital cleaning jobs.
Wait **a year or two** before moving, to see if it's real.
S3.quote: Five years is a slower car crash, but still a car crash. I'm not good at learning new stuff, so I'm not sure what I'd use the time for.
fieldNote: Extra time doesn't calm her, because she doubts her own **ability to learn**.
She wants **paid time to retrain**, not handouts forever.
Her instinct to **wait** comes from fear of choosing wrong.

steps.text: Save harder to reach four months of expenses
Ask about kitchen jobs at care homes and hospital cleaning work
Wait a year or two to see robots working before leaving Haldane
Look into government pay for people retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we'll see. At work I'd tell Bev that at least she'll be retired by then. Most people wouldn't talk about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels better, and the robots would come around 2039. Starting again at thirty-nine is a horrible age to be the new girl. My job at the biscuit factory still goes in the end, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Haldane for now and save steadily. In a few years I'd look for a job in a care home or a school kitchen, somewhere robots won't reach for a while. I'd think about doing a food hygiene certificate, because that's not too scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a quieter way. It's far away enough to put out of my head most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lukas change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talked about getting married next year. I'd still do that, but we'd keep the wedding small and keep the savings. No big party if we might both need the money later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you feel calmer about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Haldane said what it planned, honestly. The worst part is not knowing. If they said robots in 2036, I could plan around a date.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time, and **we'll see**.
I'd tease Bev that she'll be **retired by then**.
think: Privately, my job **still goes** around 2039, just later.
Starting again at **thirty-nine** feels like a horrible age.
do: Stay at Haldane for now and **save steadily**.
Move to a care home or **school kitchen** in a few years.
Take a **food hygiene certificate**, which feels manageable.
feel: **Anxious but quieter**, far enough away to ignore most days.
S4.quote: Starting again at thirty-nine is a horrible age to be the new girl. My job at the biscuit factory still goes in the end, just later.
fieldNote: The long warning **softens** her mood but doesn't remove the threat.
She picks **a small, safe course** rather than a big retrain.
She keeps **the wedding small** to protect the savings.

steps.text: Stay on the Haldane flow-wrapper for the next few years
Save steadily from each pay packet

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's too fast for someone like me, I'd just freeze. What would help is being paid while I learn something new, and Haldane telling us its plans straight instead of letting rumours go round.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the owners, not just AI. For people like me, the scary thing is a company in another city deciding we're too expensive.

headlineQuote: For people like me, the scary thing is a company in another city deciding we're too expensive.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old flow-wrapper operator** at a biscuit factory, still flustered when the film snaps.
She lives with **Lukas (her partner)**, a council bus driver, on about two and a half months of savings.
She **avoids technology**, never uses AI, and prefers to wait rather than jump.
Her steady worry is **the new owners**, who closed another factory last spring.
She runs from **uneasy to alarmed**, and the extra warning time helps only a little.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's too fast and she'd **freeze**.
whatWouldHelp: Being **paid while retraining**, and Haldane sharing its **plans** openly.
